However, it is also noted that some articles in the Chronicles of Japan regarding relations with the Korean Peninsula, such as the story of the "Seven-Branched Sword" being presented from Baekje, align with historical facts when adjusted by 120 years (two cycles of the Chinese sexagenary cycle)." {{cite kotobank|encyclopedia=Yamakawa Dictionary of Japanese History, Revised Edition|word=Empress Jingu|accessdate=2024-10-12}}.}}. In the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'', it is said that after [[Silla]] surrendered, the remaining two nations of the [[Three Han]] (Baekje and Goguryeo) also fell under Japanese control, hence the name "Three Han Expedition." However, as direct battles are recorded only against Silla, it is also referred to as the "Silla Expedition." In the ''[[Kojiki]]'', the submission of Silla and Baekje is mentioned, but there is no record of Goguryeo's reaction, and the term "Three Han" does not appear. In the ''[[Kokushi Daijiten (Shōwa era)|Kokushi Daijiten]]'' published by Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, it is listed under the entry "Silla Expedition Narrative." The "Three Han" refers to [[Mahan]] (later Baekje), [[Byeonhan]] (later [[Imna]] and [[Gaya]]), and [[Jinhan]] (later Silla), excluding Goguryeo and representing only the southern part of the Korean Peninsula. == Overview == {{Stub|date=2012nd year 1月}} {{See|Empress Jingu|Nihon Shoki}} The following is an overview of the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' account. === Oracle at Kashii Shrine and Chūai Tennō === In the 8th year of Chūai Tennō's reign (199 AD), Chūai Tennō visited Kashii Palace (modern-day [[Kashii Shrine]]) in Fukuoka's Hakata region with [[Empress Jingu]] to subjugate the [[Kumaso]] tribe. At Kashii Palace, Empress Jingu became possessed by a deity and received a divine revelation. The oracle instructed them to attack [[Silla]], a land rich with treasures, instead of the Kumaso. However, Chūai Tennō did not believe the oracle, climbed a high hill, and looked out at the sea, asking why the gods would deceive him. The deity then proclaimed that Chūai would not obtain the land but that his offspring would accomplish it. Disregarding the oracle, Chūai Tennō attacked the Kumaso but was defeated and retreated. In the 9th year of his reign (200 AD), he passed away at Kashii Palace in Tsukushi. The empress and others lamented that his death was due to ignoring the divine revelation. His body was transported by sea to Toyoura Palace for temporary burial by [[Takenouchi no Sukune]]. In the ''Amatsufumi,'' it is recorded that Chūai Tennō was struck by a Kumaso arrow. === Empress Jingu’s Expedition to Silla === [[Image:EmpressJinguInKorea.jpg|thumb|350 px|Korean Expedition. Painted by [[Tsukioka Yoshitoshi]] in 1880.]] [[Image:UtagawaKuniyoshiKaibyaku.jpg|thumb|350 px|Silla King submitting to Empress Jingu. Painted by [[Utagawa Kuniyoshi]] in 1860.]] After the sudden death of her husband Chūai Tennō (200 AD), Empress Jingu administered the government from 201 to 269 AD. In March of the 9th year of Chūai Tennō's reign, she entered the [[Saikū]] (sacred palace) as a high priestess and first subdued the Kumaso. In September, she gathered her forces and set out for the Korean Peninsula, acting on a second divine oracle from [[Sumiyoshi no Ōkami]]. Pregnant with her child (the future Ōjin Tennō), she crossed the sea to attack [[Silla]]. The kingdom surrendered without resistance, promising tribute and allegiance. Goguryeo and Baekje also pledged allegiance. During the voyage, Empress Jingu delayed childbirth by cooling her abdomen with stones called [[Tsukiyome Stones]] and [[Chinkai Stones]]. These stones were later enshrined at shrines such as [[Tsukiyomi Shrine (Iki)|Tsukiyomi Shrine]] in Iki City, Nagasaki Prefecture, and [[Chinkai Stone Hachiman Shrine]] in Itoshima City, Fukuoka Prefecture. After returning to Japan, Empress Jingu gave birth to Ōjin Tennō in Umi, Tsukushi, and changed his swaddling clothes in Shime. As a token of her conquest of Silla, she deposited a banner with eight streams at the summit of Tsushima (present-day [[Kaijin Shrine]]). The empress returned to the Kinai region after the expedition. However, her son’s half-brothers, [[Kozaka no Miko]] and [[Oshikuma no Miko]], rebelled against her in Kinai. The rebellion was suppressed by forces led by [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] and [[Tatekurakuma no Mikoto]]. The above is the core narrative shared between the ''[[Kojiki]]'' and the ''[[Nihon Shoki]].'' According to the ''Nihon Shoki,'' in addition to Silla, Goguryeo and Baekje also pledged allegiance. Silla’s king offered his prince, Misikochihatori Kan-gi, as a hostage. == Notes == * Empress Jingu is considered an important but legendary figure in Japanese history. Many aspects of her story have been examined for historical accuracy and symbolic interpretation {{draft categories| }} {{draft categories| [[Category:Three Han Campaign]] [[Category:Completion tier 1]] [[Category:qq]] [[Category:11]] }} [[sn:Three Han Campaign]] [[ja:三韓征伐]] [[ja:https://shinto.miraheze.org/wiki/Three Han Campaign?wpcategory=ZZZZZZZZZ+Unlinked#:~:text=Han%20Expedition%20(-,%E4%B8%89%E9%9F%93%E5%BE%81%E4%BC%90%2C,-Sankan%20Seibatsu)%20refers]] [[en:Three Han Campaign]] {{translated page|ja|三韓征伐|version=104412695|comment=Imported full ja history}}

Painted by [[Tsukioka Yoshitoshi]]. | conflict = Three Han Expedition | date = Unknown | place = Korean Peninsula | result = [[Yamato Kingdom]]'s expansion into the Korean Peninsula | combatant1 = [[Kofun Period|Wa]] | combatant2 = [[Three Han]]
[[Silla]] | commander1 = [[Empress Jingu]] | commander2 = Unknown | strength1 = Unknown | strength2 = Unknown | casualties1 = Unknown | casualties2 = Unknown }} '''Three Han Expedition''' (三韓征伐, ''Sankan Seibatsu'') refers to a Japanese legend in which [[Empress Jingu]], the consort of [[Chūai Tennō]] and the mother of [[Ōjin Tennō]], invaded [[Silla]] following the death of Chūai Tennō and subjugated a wide area of the [[Korean Peninsula]] (the [[Three Han]]) {{refnest|group="注"|According to Yoriko Kurazuka, [[Empress Jingu]] is described as "the consort of [[Chūai Tennō]], the protagonist of the '''Silla expedition legend''' in the Chronicles of Japan, and the mother of [[Ōjin Tennō]]." {{cite kotobank|encyclopedia=Sekai Daihyakka Jiten |word=Empress Jingu|accessdate=2024-10-12}}.}}{{refnest|group="注"|According to Yosinobu Tsukaguchi, a Ph.D. in literature and historian, the Empress Jingu legend is "a narrative of invasion of the Korean Peninsula transmitted by the court, incorporating folk traditions based on mother-and-child deity worship and the traditions of the ancient Ohotarashihime clan residing in Tsuzuki District, Kyoto Prefecture. It was further embellished by the ideology of the ancient imperial system in the 7th to 8th centuries and finally established in the Chronicles of Japan." {{cite kotobank|encyclopedia=Shogakukan Encyclopedia of Japan (Nipponica)|author=Yosinobu Tsukaguchi|word=Empress Jingu|accessdate=2024-10-12}}.}}{{refnest|group="注"|According to Yamakawa Publishing's "Yamakawa Dictionary of Japanese History, Revised Edition," Empress Jingu is a character in the Chronicles of Japan, and the narrative of the Korean expedition "was likely compiled in its present form after the late 6th century. However, it is also noted that some articles in the Chronicles of Japan regarding relations with the Korean Peninsula, such as the story of the "Seven-Branched Sword" being presented from Baekje, align with historical facts when adjusted by 120 years (two cycles of the Chinese sexagenary cycle)." {{cite kotobank|encyclopedia=Yamakawa Dictionary of Japanese History, Revised Edition|word=Empress Jingu|accessdate=2024-10-12}}.}}. In the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'', it is said that after [[Silla]] surrendered, the remaining two nations of the [[Three Han]] (Baekje and Goguryeo) also fell under Japanese control, hence the name "Three Han Expedition." However, as direct battles are recorded only against Silla, it is also referred to as the "Silla Expedition." In the ''[[Kojiki]]'', the submission of Silla and Baekje is mentioned, but there is no record of Goguryeo's reaction, and the term "Three Han" does not appear. In the ''[[Kokushi Daijiten (Shōwa era)|Kokushi Daijiten]]'' published by Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, it is listed under the entry "Silla Expedition Narrative." The "Three Han" refers to [[Mahan]] (later Baekje), [[Byeonhan]] (later [[Imna]] and [[Gaya]]), and [[Jinhan]] (later Silla), excluding Goguryeo and representing only the southern part of the Korean Peninsula. == Overview == {{Stub|date=2012nd year 1月}} {{See|Empress Jingu|Nihon Shoki}} The following is an overview of the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' account. === Oracle at Kashii Shrine and Chūai Tennō === In the 8th year of Chūai Tennō's reign (199 AD), Chūai Tennō visited Kashii Palace (modern-day [[Kashii Shrine]]) in Fukuoka's Hakata region with [[Empress Jingu]] to subjugate the [[Kumaso]] tribe. At Kashii Palace, Empress Jingu became possessed by a deity and received a divine revelation. The oracle instructed them to attack [[Silla]], a land rich with treasures, instead of the Kumaso. However, Chūai Tennō did not believe the oracle, climbed a high hill, and looked out at the sea, asking why the gods would deceive him. The deity then proclaimed that Chūai would not obtain the land but that his offspring would accomplish it. Disregarding the oracle, Chūai Tennō attacked the Kumaso but was defeated and retreated. In the 9th year of his reign (200 AD), he passed away at Kashii Palace in Tsukushi. The empress and others lamented that his death was due to ignoring the divine revelation. His body was transported by sea to Toyoura Palace for temporary burial by [[Takenouchi no Sukune]]. In the ''Amatsufumi,'' it is recorded that Chūai Tennō was struck by a Kumaso arrow. === Empress Jingu’s Expedition to Silla === [[Image:EmpressJinguInKorea.jpg|thumb|350 px|Korean Expedition. Painted by [[Tsukioka Yoshitoshi]] in 1880.]] [[Image:UtagawaKuniyoshiKaibyaku.jpg|thumb|350 px|Silla King submitting to Empress Jingu. Painted by [[Utagawa Kuniyoshi]] in 1860.]] After the sudden death of her husband Chūai Tennō (200 AD), Empress Jingu administered the government from 201 to 269 AD. In March of the 9th year of Chūai Tennō's reign, she entered the [[Saikū]] (sacred palace) as a high priestess and first subdued the Kumaso. In September, she gathered her forces and set out for the Korean Peninsula, acting on a second divine oracle from [[Sumiyoshi no Ōkami]]. Pregnant with her child (the future Ōjin Tennō), she crossed the sea to attack [[Silla]]. The kingdom surrendered without resistance, promising tribute and allegiance. Goguryeo and Baekje also pledged allegiance. During the voyage, Empress Jingu delayed childbirth by cooling her abdomen with stones called [[Tsukiyome Stones]] and [[Chinkai Stones]]. These stones were later enshrined at shrines such as [[Tsukiyomi Shrine (Iki)|Tsukiyomi Shrine]] in Iki City, Nagasaki Prefecture, and [[Chinkai Stone Hachiman Shrine]] in Itoshima City, Fukuoka Prefecture. After returning to Japan, Empress Jingu gave birth to Ōjin Tennō in Umi, Tsukushi, and changed his swaddling clothes in Shime. As a token of her conquest of Silla, she deposited a banner with eight streams at the summit of Tsushima (present-day [[Kaijin Shrine]]). The empress returned to the Kinai region after the expedition. However, her son’s half-brothers, [[Kozaka no Miko]] and [[Oshikuma no Miko]], rebelled against her in Kinai. The rebellion was suppressed by forces led by [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] and [[Tatekurakuma no Mikoto]]. The above is the core narrative shared between the ''[[Kojiki]]'' and the ''[[Nihon Shoki]].'' According to the ''Nihon Shoki,'' in addition to Silla, Goguryeo and Baekje also pledged allegiance. Silla’s king offered his prince, Misikochihatori Kan-gi, as a hostage. == Notes == * Empress Jingu is considered an important but legendary figure in Japanese history. Many aspects of her story have been examined for historical accuracy and symbolic interpretation {{translated page|ja|三韓征伐|version=104412695|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Completion tier 1]] }} [[sn:Three Han Campaign]] [[ja:三韓征伐]] [[ja:https://shinto.miraheze.org/wiki/Three Han Campaign?wpcategory=ZZZZZZZZZ+Unlinked#:~:text=Han%20Expedition%20(-,%E4%B8%89%E9%9F%93%E5%BE%81%E4%BC%90%2C,-Sankan%20Seibatsu)%20refers]] [[en:Three Han Campaign]]

However, Chūai Tennō did not believe the oracle, climbed a high hill, and looked out at the sea, asking why the gods would deceive him. Painted by [[Tsukioka Yoshitoshi]]. | conflict = Three Han Expedition | date = Unknown | place = Korean Peninsula | result = [[Yamato Kingdom]]'s expansion into the Korean Peninsula | combatant1 = [[Kofun Period|Wa]] | combatant2 = [[Three Han]]
[[Silla]] | commander1 = [[Empress Jingu]] | commander2 = Unknown | strength1 = Unknown | strength2 = Unknown | casualties1 = Unknown | casualties2 = Unknown }} '''Three Han Expedition''' (三韓征伐, ''Sankan Seibatsu'') refers to a Japanese legend in which [[Empress Jingu]], the consort of [[Chūai Tennō]] and the mother of [[Ōjin Tennō]], invaded [[Silla]] following the death of Chūai Tennō and subjugated a wide area of the [[Korean Peninsula]] (the [[Three Han]]) {{refnest|group="注"|According to Yoriko Kurazuka, [[Empress Jingu]] is described as "the consort of [[Chūai Tennō]], the protagonist of the '''Silla expedition legend''' in the Chronicles of Japan, and the mother of [[Ōjin Tennō]]." {{cite kotobank|encyclopedia=Sekai Daihyakka Jiten |word=Empress Jingu|accessdate=2024-10-12}}.}}{{refnest|group="注"|According to Yosinobu Tsukaguchi, a Ph.D. in literature and historian, the Empress Jingu legend is "a narrative of invasion of the Korean Peninsula transmitted by the court, incorporating folk traditions based on mother-and-child deity worship and the traditions of the ancient Ohotarashihime clan residing in Tsuzuki District, Kyoto Prefecture. It was further embellished by the ideology of the ancient imperial system in the 7th to 8th centuries and finally established in the Chronicles of Japan." {{cite kotobank|encyclopedia=Shogakukan Encyclopedia of Japan (Nipponica)|author=Yosinobu Tsukaguchi|word=Empress Jingu|accessdate=2024-10-12}}.}}{{refnest|group="注"|According to Yamakawa Publishing's "Yamakawa Dictionary of Japanese History, Revised Edition," Empress Jingu is a character in the Chronicles of Japan, and the narrative of the Korean expedition "was likely compiled in its present form after the late 6th century. However, it is also noted that some articles in the Chronicles of Japan regarding relations with the Korean Peninsula, such as the story of the "Seven-Branched Sword" being presented from Baekje, align with historical facts when adjusted by 120 years (two cycles of the Chinese sexagenary cycle)." {{cite kotobank|encyclopedia=Yamakawa Dictionary of Japanese History, Revised Edition|word=Empress Jingu|accessdate=2024-10-12}}.}}. In the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'', it is said that after [[Silla]] surrendered, the remaining two nations of the [[Three Han]] (Baekje and Goguryeo) also fell under Japanese control, hence the name "Three Han Expedition." However, as direct battles are recorded only against Silla, it is also referred to as the "Silla Expedition." In the ''[[Kojiki]]'', the submission of Silla and Baekje is mentioned, but there is no record of Goguryeo's reaction, and the term "Three Han" does not appear. In the ''[[Kokushi Daijiten (Shōwa era)|Kokushi Daijiten]]'' published by Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, it is listed under the entry "Silla Expedition Narrative." The "Three Han" refers to [[Mahan]] (later Baekje), [[Byeonhan]] (later [[Imna]] and [[Gaya]]), and [[Jinhan]] (later Silla), excluding Goguryeo and representing only the southern part of the Korean Peninsula. == Overview == {{Stub|date=2012nd year 1月}} {{See|Empress Jingu|Nihon Shoki}} The following is an overview of the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' account. === Oracle at Kashii Shrine and Chūai Tennō === In the 8th year of Chūai Tennō's reign (199 AD), Chūai Tennō visited Kashii Palace (modern-day [[Kashii Shrine]]) in Fukuoka's Hakata region with [[Empress Jingu]] to subjugate the [[Kumaso]] tribe. At Kashii Palace, Empress Jingu became possessed by a deity and received a divine revelation. The oracle instructed them to attack [[Silla]], a land rich with treasures, instead of the Kumaso. However, Chūai Tennō did not believe the oracle, climbed a high hill, and looked out at the sea, asking why the gods would deceive him. The deity then proclaimed that Chūai would not obtain the land but that his offspring would accomplish it. Disregarding the oracle, Chūai Tennō attacked the Kumaso but was defeated and retreated. In the 9th year of his reign (200 AD), he passed away at Kashii Palace in Tsukushi. The empress and others lamented that his death was due to ignoring the divine revelation. His body was transported by sea to Toyoura Palace for temporary burial by [[Takenouchi no Sukune]]. In the ''Amatsufumi,'' it is recorded that Chūai Tennō was struck by a Kumaso arrow. === Empress Jingu’s Expedition to Silla === [[Image:EmpressJinguInKorea.jpg|thumb|350 px|Korean Expedition. Painted by [[Tsukioka Yoshitoshi]] in 1880.]] [[Image:UtagawaKuniyoshiKaibyaku.jpg|thumb|350 px|Silla King submitting to Empress Jingu. Painted by [[Utagawa Kuniyoshi]] in 1860.]] After the sudden death of her husband Chūai Tennō (200 AD), Empress Jingu administered the government from 201 to 269 AD. In March of the 9th year of Chūai Tennō's reign, she entered the [[Saikū]] (sacred palace) as a high priestess and first subdued the Kumaso. In September, she gathered her forces and set out for the Korean Peninsula, acting on a second divine oracle from [[Sumiyoshi no Ōkami]]. Pregnant with her child (the future Ōjin Tennō), she crossed the sea to attack [[Silla]]. The kingdom surrendered without resistance, promising tribute and allegiance. Goguryeo and Baekje also pledged allegiance. During the voyage, Empress Jingu delayed childbirth by cooling her abdomen with stones called [[Tsukiyome Stones]] and [[Chinkai Stones]]. These stones were later enshrined at shrines such as [[Tsukiyomi Shrine (Iki)|Tsukiyomi Shrine]] in Iki City, Nagasaki Prefecture, and [[Chinkai Stone Hachiman Shrine]] in Itoshima City, Fukuoka Prefecture. After returning to Japan, Empress Jingu gave birth to Ōjin Tennō in Umi, Tsukushi, and changed his swaddling clothes in Shime. As a token of her conquest of Silla, she deposited a banner with eight streams at the summit of Tsushima (present-day [[Kaijin Shrine]]). The empress returned to the Kinai region after the expedition. However, her son’s half-brothers, [[Kozaka no Miko]] and [[Oshikuma no Miko]], rebelled against her in Kinai. The rebellion was suppressed by forces led by [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] and [[Tatekurakuma no Mikoto]]. The above is the core narrative shared between the ''[[Kojiki]]'' and the ''[[Nihon Shoki]].'' According to the ''Nihon Shoki,'' in addition to Silla, Goguryeo and Baekje also pledged allegiance. Silla’s king offered his prince, Misikochihatori Kan-gi, as a hostage. == Notes == * Empress Jingu is considered an important but legendary figure in Japanese history. Many aspects of her story have been examined for historical accuracy and symbolic interpretation {{translated page|ja|三韓征伐|version=104412695|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Completion tier 1]] }} [[sn:Three Han Campaign]] [[ja:三韓征伐]] [[ja:https://shinto.miraheze.org/wiki/Three Han Campaign?wpcategory=ZZZZZZZZZ+Unlinked#:~:text=Han%20Expedition%20(-,%E4%B8%89%E9%9F%93%E5%BE%81%E4%BC%90%2C,-Sankan%20Seibatsu)%20refers]] [[en:Three Han Campaign]] [[Category:Pseudohistory]] [[Category:古代日朝関係]] [[Category:Kofun period]] [[Category:Historiography of Japan]] [[Category:Wars involving Japan]] [[Category:Wars involving Korea]] [[Category:神功皇后]]

{{Battlebox | battle_name = Three Han Expedition | campaign = |colour_scheme = background:#ffccaa | image = [[Image:Empress Jingu and Takenouchi no Sukune Fishing at Chikuzen LACMA M.84.31.260.jpg|200px]] | caption = Empress Jingu and Takenouchi no Sukune practicing fishing divination before the conquest of Silla. Painted by [[Tsukioka Yoshitoshi]]. | conflict = Three Han Expedition | date = Unknown | place = Korean Peninsula | result = [[Yamato Kingdom]]'s expansion into the Korean Peninsula | combatant1 = [[Kofun Period|Wa]] | combatant2 = [[Three Han]]
[[Silla]] | commander1 = [[Empress Jingu]] | commander2 = Unknown | strength1 = Unknown | strength2 = Unknown | casualties1 = Unknown | casualties2 = Unknown }} '''Three Han Expedition''' (三韓征伐, ''Sankan Seibatsu'') refers to a Japanese legend in which [[Empress Jingu]], the consort of [[Chūai Tennō]] and the mother of [[Ōjin Tennō]], invaded [[Silla]] following the death of Chūai Tennō and subjugated a wide area of the [[Korean Peninsula]] (the [[Three Han]]) {{refnest|group="注"|According to Yoriko Kurazuka, [[Empress Jingu]] is described as "the consort of [[Chūai Tennō]], the protagonist of the '''Silla expedition legend''' in the Chronicles of Japan, and the mother of [[Ōjin Tennō]]." {{cite kotobank|encyclopedia=Sekai Daihyakka Jiten |word=Empress Jingu|accessdate=2024-10-12}}.}}{{refnest|group="注"|According to Yosinobu Tsukaguchi, a Ph.D. in literature and historian, the Empress Jingu legend is "a narrative of invasion of the Korean Peninsula transmitted by the court, incorporating folk traditions based on mother-and-child deity worship and the traditions of the ancient Ohotarashihime clan residing in Tsuzuki District, Kyoto Prefecture. It was further embellished by the ideology of the ancient imperial system in the 7th to 8th centuries and finally established in the Chronicles of Japan." {{cite kotobank|encyclopedia=Shogakukan Encyclopedia of Japan (Nipponica)|author=Yosinobu Tsukaguchi|word=Empress Jingu|accessdate=2024-10-12}}.}}{{refnest|group="注"|According to Yamakawa Publishing's "Yamakawa Dictionary of Japanese History, Revised Edition," Empress Jingu is a character in the Chronicles of Japan, and the narrative of the Korean expedition "was likely compiled in its present form after the late 6th century. However, it is also noted that some articles in the Chronicles of Japan regarding relations with the Korean Peninsula, such as the story of the "Seven-Branched Sword" being presented from Baekje, align with historical facts when adjusted by 120 years (two cycles of the Chinese sexagenary cycle)." {{cite kotobank|encyclopedia=Yamakawa Dictionary of Japanese History, Revised Edition|word=Empress Jingu|accessdate=2024-10-12}}.}}. In the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'', it is said that after [[Silla]] surrendered, the remaining two nations of the [[Three Han]] (Baekje and Goguryeo) also fell under Japanese control, hence the name "Three Han Expedition." However, as direct battles are recorded only against Silla, it is also referred to as the "Silla Expedition." In the ''[[Kojiki]]'', the submission of Silla and Baekje is mentioned, but there is no record of Goguryeo's reaction, and the term "Three Han" does not appear. In the ''[[Kokushi Daijiten (Shōwa era)|Kokushi Daijiten]]'' published by Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, it is listed under the entry "Silla Expedition Narrative." The "Three Han" refers to [[Mahan]] (later Baekje), [[Byeonhan]] (later [[Imna]] and [[Gaya]]), and [[Jinhan]] (later Silla), excluding Goguryeo and representing only the southern part of the Korean Peninsula. == Overview == {{Stub|date=2012nd year 1月}} {{See|Empress Jingu|Nihon Shoki}} The following is an overview of the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' account. === Oracle at Kashii Shrine and Chūai Tennō === In the 8th year of Chūai Tennō's reign (199 AD), Chūai Tennō visited Kashii Palace (modern-day [[Kashii Shrine]]) in Fukuoka's Hakata region with [[Empress Jingu]] to subjugate the [[Kumaso]] tribe. At Kashii Palace, Empress Jingu became possessed by a deity and received a divine revelation. The oracle instructed them to attack [[Silla]], a land rich with treasures, instead of the Kumaso. However, Chūai Tennō did not believe the oracle, climbed a high hill, and looked out at the sea, asking why the gods would deceive him. The deity then proclaimed that Chūai would not obtain the land but that his offspring would accomplish it. Disregarding the oracle, Chūai Tennō attacked the Kumaso but was defeated and retreated. In the 9th year of his reign (200 AD), he passed away at Kashii Palace in Tsukushi. The empress and others lamented that his death was due to ignoring the divine revelation. His body was transported by sea to Toyoura Palace for temporary burial by [[Takenouchi no Sukune]]. In the ''Amatsufumi,'' it is recorded that Chūai Tennō was struck by a Kumaso arrow. === Empress Jingu’s Expedition to Silla === [[Image:EmpressJinguInKorea.jpg|thumb|350 px|Korean Expedition. Painted by [[Tsukioka Yoshitoshi]] in 1880.]] [[Image:UtagawaKuniyoshiKaibyaku.jpg|thumb|350 px|Silla King submitting to Empress Jingu. Painted by [[Utagawa Kuniyoshi]] in 1860.]] After the sudden death of her husband Chūai Tennō (200 AD), Empress Jingu administered the government from 201 to 269 AD. In March of the 9th year of Chūai Tennō's reign, she entered the [[Saikū]] (sacred palace) as a high priestess and first subdued the Kumaso. In September, she gathered her forces and set out for the Korean Peninsula, acting on a second divine oracle from [[Sumiyoshi no Ōkami]]. Pregnant with her child (the future Ōjin Tennō), she crossed the sea to attack [[Silla]]. The kingdom surrendered without resistance, promising tribute and allegiance. Goguryeo and Baekje also pledged allegiance. During the voyage, Empress Jingu delayed childbirth by cooling her abdomen with stones called [[Tsukiyome Stones]] and [[Chinkai Stones]]. These stones were later enshrined at shrines such as [[Tsukiyomi Shrine (Iki)|Tsukiyomi Shrine]] in Iki City, Nagasaki Prefecture, and [[Chinkai Stone Hachiman Shrine]] in Itoshima City, Fukuoka Prefecture. After returning to Japan, Empress Jingu gave birth to Ōjin Tennō in Umi, Tsukushi, and changed his swaddling clothes in Shime. As a token of her conquest of Silla, she deposited a banner with eight streams at the summit of Tsushima (present-day [[Kaijin Shrine]]). The empress returned to the Kinai region after the expedition. However, her son’s half-brothers, [[Kozaka no Miko]] and [[Oshikuma no Miko]], rebelled against her in Kinai. The rebellion was suppressed by forces led by [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] and [[Tatekurakuma no Mikoto]]. The above is the core narrative shared between the ''[[Kojiki]]'' and the ''[[Nihon Shoki]].'' According to the ''Nihon Shoki,'' in addition to Silla, Goguryeo and Baekje also pledged allegiance. Silla’s king offered his prince, Misikochihatori Kan-gi, as a hostage. == Notes == * Empress Jingu is considered an important but legendary figure in Japanese history. Many aspects of her story have been examined for historical accuracy and symbolic interpretation {{translated page|ja|三韓征伐|version=104412695|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Completion tier 1]] }} [[sn:Three Han Campaign]] [[ja:三韓征伐]] [[ja:https://shinto.miraheze.org/wiki/Three Han Campaign?wpcategory=ZZZZZZZZZ+Unlinked#:~:text=Han%20Expedition%20(-,%E4%B8%89%E9%9F%93%E5%BE%81%E4%BC%90%2C,-Sankan%20Seibatsu)%20refers]] [[Category:Pseudohistory]] [[Category:古代日朝関係]] [[Category:Kofun period]] [[Category:Historiography of Japan]] [[Category:Wars involving Japan]] [[Category:Wars involving Korea]] [[Category:Empress Jingū]] [[ko:삼한 정벌]] [[zh:三韩征伐]]

[[Silla]] | commander1 = [[Empress Jingu]] | commander2 = Unknown | strength1 = Unknown | strength2 = Unknown | casualties1 = Unknown | casualties2 = Unknown }} '''Three Han Expedition''' (三韓征伐, ''Sankan Seibatsu'') refers to a Japanese legend in which [[Empress Jingu]], the consort of [[:en:Chūai Tennō|Chūai Tennō]] and the mother of [[:en:Ōjin Tennō|Ōjin Tennō]], invaded [[Silla]] following the death of Chūai Tennō and subjugated a wide area of the [[Korean Peninsula]] (the [[Three Han]]) {{refnest|group="注"|According to Yoriko Kurazuka, [[Empress Jingu]] is described as "the consort of [[:en:Chūai Tennō|Chūai Tennō]], the protagonist of the '''Silla expedition legend''' in the Chronicles of Japan, and the mother of [[:en:Ōjin Tennō|Ōjin Tennō]]." {{cite kotobank|encyclopedia=Sekai Daihyakka Jiten |word=Empress Jingu|accessdate=2024-10-12}}.}}{{refnest|group="注"|According to Yosinobu Tsukaguchi, a Ph.D. in literature and historian, the Empress Jingu legend is "a narrative of invasion of the Korean Peninsula transmitted by the court, incorporating folk traditions based on mother-and-child deity worship and the traditions of the ancient Ohotarashihime clan residing in Tsuzuki District, Kyoto Prefecture. It was further embellished by the ideology of the ancient imperial system in the 7th to 8th centuries and finally established in the Chronicles of Japan." {{cite kotobank|encyclopedia=Shogakukan Encyclopedia of Japan (Nipponica)|author=Yosinobu Tsukaguchi|word=Empress Jingu|accessdate=2024-10-12}}.}}{{refnest|group="注"|According to Yamakawa Publishing's "Yamakawa Dictionary of Japanese History, Revised Edition," Empress Jingu is a character in the Chronicles of Japan, and the narrative of the Korean expedition "was likely compiled in its present form after the late 6th century. However, it is also noted that some articles in the Chronicles of Japan regarding relations with the Korean Peninsula, such as the story of the "Seven-Branched Sword" being presented from Baekje, align with historical facts when adjusted by 120 years (two cycles of the Chinese sexagenary cycle)." {{cite kotobank|encyclopedia=Yamakawa Dictionary of Japanese History, Revised Edition|word=Empress Jingu|accessdate=2024-10-12}}.}}. In the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'', it is said that after [[Silla]] surrendered, the remaining two nations of the [[Three Han]] (Baekje and Goguryeo) also fell under Japanese control, hence the name "Three Han Expedition." However, as direct battles are recorded only against Silla, it is also referred to as the "Silla Expedition." In the ''[[Kojiki]]'', the submission of Silla and Baekje is mentioned, but there is no record of Goguryeo's reaction, and the term "Three Han" does not appear. In the ''[[Kokushi Daijiten (Shōwa era)|Kokushi Daijiten]]'' published by Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, it is listed under the entry "Silla Expedition Narrative." The "Three Han" refers to [[Mahan]] (later Baekje), [[Byeonhan]] (later [[Imna]] and [[:en:Gaya|Gaya]]), and [[Jinhan]] (later Silla), excluding Goguryeo and representing only the southern part of the Korean Peninsula. == Overview == {{Stub|date=2012nd year 1月}} {{See|Empress Jingu|Nihon Shoki}} The following is an overview of the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' account. === Oracle at Kashii Shrine and Chūai Tennō === In the 8th year of Chūai Tennō's reign (199 AD), Chūai Tennō visited Kashii Palace (modern-day [[Kashii Shrine]]) in Fukuoka's Hakata region with [[Empress Jingu]] to subjugate the [[Kumaso]] tribe. At Kashii Palace, Empress Jingu became possessed by a deity and received a divine revelation. The oracle instructed them to attack [[Silla]], a land rich with treasures, instead of the Kumaso. However, Chūai Tennō did not believe the oracle, climbed a high hill, and looked out at the sea, asking why the gods would deceive him. The deity then proclaimed that Chūai would not obtain the land but that his offspring would accomplish it. Disregarding the oracle, Chūai Tennō attacked the Kumaso but was defeated and retreated. In the 9th year of his reign (200 AD), he passed away at Kashii Palace in Tsukushi. The empress and others lamented that his death was due to ignoring the divine revelation. His body was transported by sea to Toyoura Palace for temporary burial by [[Takenouchi no Sukune]]. In the ''Amatsufumi,'' it is recorded that Chūai Tennō was struck by a Kumaso arrow. === Empress Jingu’s Expedition to Silla === [[Image:EmpressJinguInKorea.jpg|thumb|350 px|Korean Expedition. Painted by [[Tsukioka Yoshitoshi]] in 1880.]] [[Image:UtagawaKuniyoshiKaibyaku.jpg|thumb|350 px|Silla King submitting to Empress Jingu. Painted by [[Utagawa Kuniyoshi]] in 1860.]] After the sudden death of her husband Chūai Tennō (200 AD), Empress Jingu administered the government from 201 to 269 AD. In March of the 9th year of Chūai Tennō's reign, she entered the [[Saikū]] (sacred palace) as a high priestess and first subdued the Kumaso. In September, she gathered her forces and set out for the Korean Peninsula, acting on a second divine oracle from [[Sumiyoshi no Ōkami]]. Pregnant with her child (the future Ōjin Tennō), she crossed the sea to attack [[Silla]]. The kingdom surrendered without resistance, promising tribute and allegiance. Goguryeo and Baekje also pledged allegiance. During the voyage, Empress Jingu delayed childbirth by cooling her abdomen with stones called [[Tsukiyome Stones]] and [[Chinkai Stones]]. These stones were later enshrined at shrines such as [[Tsukiyomi Shrine (Iki)|Tsukiyomi Shrine]] in Iki City, Nagasaki Prefecture, and [[Chinkai Stone Hachiman Shrine]] in Itoshima City, Fukuoka Prefecture. After returning to Japan, Empress Jingu gave birth to Ōjin Tennō in Umi, Tsukushi, and changed his swaddling clothes in Shime. As a token of her conquest of Silla, she deposited a banner with eight streams at the summit of Tsushima (present-day [[Kaijin Shrine]]). The empress returned to the Kinai region after the expedition. However, her son’s half-brothers, [[Kozaka no Miko]] and [[Oshikuma no Miko]], rebelled against her in Kinai. The rebellion was suppressed by forces led by [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] and [[Tatekurakuma no Mikoto]]. The above is the core narrative shared between the ''[[Kojiki]]'' and the ''[[Nihon Shoki]].'' According to the ''Nihon Shoki,'' in addition to Silla, Goguryeo and Baekje also pledged allegiance. Silla’s king offered his prince, Misikochihatori Kan-gi, as a hostage. == Notes == * Empress Jingu is considered an important but legendary figure in Japanese history. Many aspects of her story have been examined for historical accuracy and symbolic interpretation {{translated page|ja|三韓征伐|version=104412695|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Completion tier 1]] }} [[sn:Three Han Campaign]] [[ja:三韓征伐]] [[ja:https://shinto.miraheze.org/wiki/Three Han Campaign?wpcategory=ZZZZZZZZZ+Unlinked#:~:text=Han%20Expedition%20(-,%E4%B8%89%E9%9F%93%E5%BE%81%E4%BC%90%2C,-Sankan%20Seibatsu)%20refers]] [[Category:Pseudohistory]] [[Category:古代日朝関係]] [[Category:Kofun period]] [[Category:Historiography of Japan]] [[Category:Wars involving Japan]] [[Category:Wars involving Korea]] [[Category:Empress Jingū]] [[ko:삼한 정벌]] [[zh:三韩征伐]]

However, Chūai Tennō did not believe the oracle, climbed a high hill, and looked out at the sea, asking why the gods would deceive him. The deity then proclaimed that Chūai would not obtain the land but that his offspring would accomplish it. Disregarding the oracle, Chūai Tennō attacked the Kumaso but was defeated and retreated. In the 9th year of his reign (200 AD), he passed away at Kashii Palace in Tsukushi. The empress and others lamented that his death was due to ignoring the divine revelation. His body was transported by sea to Toyoura Palace for temporary burial by [[Takenouchi no Sukune]]. Painted by [[Tsukioka Yoshitoshi]] in 1880.]] [[Image:UtagawaKuniyoshiKaibyaku.jpg|thumb|350 px|Silla King submitting to Empress Jingu. Painted by [[Utagawa Kuniyoshi]] in 1860.]] After the sudden death of her husband Chūai Tennō (200 AD), Empress Jingu administered the government from 201 to 269 AD. In March of the 9th year of Chūai Tennō's reign, she entered the [[Saikū]] (sacred palace) as a high priestess and first subdued the Kumaso. In September, she gathered her forces and set out for the Korean Peninsula, acting on a second divine oracle from [[Sumiyoshi no Ōkami]]. {{Battlebox | battle_name = Three Han Expedition | campaign = |colour_scheme = background:#ffccaa | image = [[Image:Empress Jingu and Takenouchi no Sukune Fishing at Chikuzen LACMA M.84.31.260.jpg|200px]] | caption = Empress Jingu and Takenouchi no Sukune practicing fishing divination before the conquest of Silla. Painted by [[Tsukioka Yoshitoshi]]. | conflict = Three Han Expedition | date = Unknown | place = Korean Peninsula | result = [[Yamato Kingdom]]'s expansion into the Korean Peninsula | combatant1 = [[Kofun Period|Wa]] | combatant2 = [[Three Han]]
[[Silla]] | commander1 = [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]] | commander2 = Unknown | strength1 = Unknown | strength2 = Unknown | casualties1 = Unknown | casualties2 = Unknown }} '''Three Han Expedition''' (三韓征伐, ''Sankan Seibatsu'') refers to a Japanese legend in which [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]], the consort of [[:en:Chūai Tennō|Chūai Tennō]] and the mother of [[:en:Ōjin Tennō|Ōjin Tennō]], invaded [[Silla]] following the death of Chūai Tennō and subjugated a wide area of the [[:en:Korea|Korea]] (the [[Three Han]]) {{refnest|group="注"|According to Yoriko Kurazuka, [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]] is described as "the consort of [[:en:Chūai Tennō|Chūai Tennō]], the protagonist of the '''Silla expedition legend''' in the Chronicles of Japan, and the mother of [[:en:Ōjin Tennō|Ōjin Tennō]]." {{cite kotobank|encyclopedia=Sekai Daihyakka Jiten |word=Empress Jingu|accessdate=2024-10-12}}.}}{{refnest|group="注"|According to Yosinobu Tsukaguchi, a Ph.D. in literature and historian, the Empress Jingu legend is "a narrative of invasion of the Korean Peninsula transmitted by the court, incorporating folk traditions based on mother-and-child deity worship and the traditions of the ancient Ohotarashihime clan residing in Tsuzuki District, Kyoto Prefecture. It was further embellished by the ideology of the ancient imperial system in the 7th to 8th centuries and finally established in the Chronicles of Japan." {{cite kotobank|encyclopedia=Shogakukan Encyclopedia of Japan (Nipponica)|author=Yosinobu Tsukaguchi|word=Empress Jingu|accessdate=2024-10-12}}.}}{{refnest|group="注"|According to Yamakawa Publishing's "Yamakawa Dictionary of Japanese History, Revised Edition," Empress Jingu is a character in the Chronicles of Japan, and the narrative of the Korean expedition "was likely compiled in its present form after the late 6th century. However, it is also noted that some articles in the Chronicles of Japan regarding relations with the Korean Peninsula, such as the story of the "Seven-Branched Sword" being presented from Baekje, align with historical facts when adjusted by 120 years (two cycles of the Chinese sexagenary cycle)." {{cite kotobank|encyclopedia=Yamakawa Dictionary of Japanese History, Revised Edition|word=Empress Jingu|accessdate=2024-10-12}}.}}. In the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'', it is said that after [[Silla]] surrendered, the remaining two nations of the [[Three Han]] (Baekje and Goguryeo) also fell under Japanese control, hence the name "Three Han Expedition." However, as direct battles are recorded only against Silla, it is also referred to as the "Silla Expedition." In the ''[[Kojiki]]'', the submission of Silla and Baekje is mentioned, but there is no record of Goguryeo's reaction, and the term "Three Han" does not appear. In the ''[[Kokushi Daijiten (Shōwa era)|Kokushi Daijiten]]'' published by Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, it is listed under the entry "Silla Expedition Narrative." The "Three Han" refers to [[:en:Mahan|Mahan]] (later Baekje), [[:en:Byeonhan|Byeonhan]] (later [[:en:Imna|Imna]] and [[:en:Gaya|Gaya]]), and [[:en:Jinhan|Jinhan]] (later Silla), excluding Goguryeo and representing only the southern part of the Korean Peninsula. == Overview == {{Stub|date=2012nd year 1月}} {{See|Empress Jingu|Nihon Shoki}} The following is an overview of the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' account. === Oracle at Kashii Shrine and Chūai Tennō === In the 8th year of Chūai Tennō's reign (199 AD), Chūai Tennō visited Kashii Palace (modern-day [[Kashii Shrine]]) in Fukuoka's Hakata region with [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]] to subjugate the [[Kumaso]] tribe. At Kashii Palace, Empress Jingu became possessed by a deity and received a divine revelation. The oracle instructed them to attack [[Silla]], a land rich with treasures, instead of the Kumaso. However, Chūai Tennō did not believe the oracle, climbed a high hill, and looked out at the sea, asking why the gods would deceive him. The deity then proclaimed that Chūai would not obtain the land but that his offspring would accomplish it. Disregarding the oracle, Chūai Tennō attacked the Kumaso but was defeated and retreated. In the 9th year of his reign (200 AD), he passed away at Kashii Palace in Tsukushi. The empress and others lamented that his death was due to ignoring the divine revelation. His body was transported by sea to Toyoura Palace for temporary burial by [[Takenouchi no Sukune]]. In the ''Amatsufumi,'' it is recorded that Chūai Tennō was struck by a Kumaso arrow. === Empress Jingu’s Expedition to Silla === [[Image:EmpressJinguInKorea.jpg|thumb|350 px|Korean Expedition. Painted by [[Tsukioka Yoshitoshi]] in 1880.]] [[Image:UtagawaKuniyoshiKaibyaku.jpg|thumb|350 px|Silla King submitting to Empress Jingu. Painted by [[Utagawa Kuniyoshi]] in 1860.]] After the sudden death of her husband Chūai Tennō (200 AD), Empress Jingu administered the government from 201 to 269 AD. In March of the 9th year of Chūai Tennō's reign, she entered the [[Saikū]] (sacred palace) as a high priestess and first subdued the Kumaso. In September, she gathered her forces and set out for the Korean Peninsula, acting on a second divine oracle from [[Sumiyoshi no Ōkami]]. Pregnant with her child (the future Ōjin Tennō), she crossed the sea to attack [[Silla]]. The kingdom surrendered without resistance, promising tribute and allegiance. Goguryeo and Baekje also pledged allegiance. During the voyage, Empress Jingu delayed childbirth by cooling her abdomen with stones called [[Tsukiyome Stones]] and [[Chinkai Stones]]. These stones were later enshrined at shrines such as [[Tsukiyomi Shrine (Iki)|Tsukiyomi Shrine]] in Iki City, Nagasaki Prefecture, and [[Chinkai Stone Hachiman Shrine]] in Itoshima City, Fukuoka Prefecture. After returning to Japan, Empress Jingu gave birth to Ōjin Tennō in Umi, Tsukushi, and changed his swaddling clothes in Shime. As a token of her conquest of Silla, she deposited a banner with eight streams at the summit of Tsushima (present-day [[Kaijin Shrine]]). The empress returned to the Kinai region after the expedition. However, her son’s half-brothers, [[Kozaka no Miko]] and [[Oshikuma no Miko]], rebelled against her in Kinai. The rebellion was suppressed by forces led by [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] and [[Tatekurakuma no Mikoto]]. The above is the core narrative shared between the ''[[Kojiki]]'' and the ''[[Nihon Shoki]].'' According to the ''Nihon Shoki,'' in addition to Silla, Goguryeo and Baekje also pledged allegiance. Silla’s king offered his prince, Misikochihatori Kan-gi, as a hostage. == Notes == * Empress Jingu is considered an important but legendary figure in Japanese history. Many aspects of her story have been examined for historical accuracy and symbolic interpretation {{translated page|ja|三韓征伐|version=104412695|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Completion tier 1]] }} [[sn:Three Han Campaign]] [[ja:三韓征伐]] [[ja:https://shinto.miraheze.org/wiki/Three Han Campaign?wpcategory=ZZZZZZZZZ+Unlinked#:~:text=Han%20Expedition%20(-,%E4%B8%89%E9%9F%93%E5%BE%81%E4%BC%90%2C,-Sankan%20Seibatsu)%20refers]] [[Category:Pseudohistory]] [[Category:Japan–Korea Relations in Antiquity]] [[Category:Kofun period]] [[Category:Historiography of Japan]] [[Category:Wars involving Japan]] [[Category:Wars involving Korea]] [[Category:Empress Jingū]] [[ko:삼한 정벌]] [[zh:三韩征伐]]

[[:en:Silla|Silla]] | commander1 = [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]] | commander2 = Unknown | strength1 = Unknown | strength2 = Unknown | casualties1 = Unknown | casualties2 = Unknown }} '''Three Han Expedition''' (三韓征伐, ''Sankan Seibatsu'') refers to a Japanese legend in which [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]], the consort of [[:en:Chūai Tennō|Chūai Tennō]] and the mother of [[:en:Ōjin Tennō|Ōjin Tennō]], invaded [[:en:Silla|Silla]] following the death of Chūai Tennō and subjugated a wide area of the [[:en:Korea|Korea]] (the [[:en:Three Han|Three Han]]) {{refnest|group="注"|According to Yoriko Kurazuka, [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]] is described as "the consort of [[:en:Chūai Tennō|Chūai Tennō]], the protagonist of the '''Silla expedition legend''' in the Chronicles of Japan, and the mother of [[:en:Ōjin Tennō|Ōjin Tennō]]." {{cite kotobank|encyclopedia=Sekai Daihyakka Jiten |word=Empress Jingu|accessdate=2024-10-12}}.}}{{refnest|group="注"|According to Yosinobu Tsukaguchi, a Ph.D. in literature and historian, the Empress Jingu legend is "a narrative of invasion of the Korean Peninsula transmitted by the court, incorporating folk traditions based on mother-and-child deity worship and the traditions of the ancient Ohotarashihime clan residing in Tsuzuki District, Kyoto Prefecture. It was further embellished by the ideology of the ancient imperial system in the 7th to 8th centuries and finally established in the Chronicles of Japan." {{cite kotobank|encyclopedia=Shogakukan Encyclopedia of Japan (Nipponica)|author=Yosinobu Tsukaguchi|word=Empress Jingu|accessdate=2024-10-12}}.}}{{refnest|group="注"|According to Yamakawa Publishing's "Yamakawa Dictionary of Japanese History, Revised Edition," Empress Jingu is a character in the Chronicles of Japan, and the narrative of the Korean expedition "was likely compiled in its present form after the late 6th century. However, it is also noted that some articles in the Chronicles of Japan regarding relations with the Korean Peninsula, such as the story of the "Seven-Branched Sword" being presented from Baekje, align with historical facts when adjusted by 120 years (two cycles of the Chinese sexagenary cycle)." {{cite kotobank|encyclopedia=Yamakawa Dictionary of Japanese History, Revised Edition|word=Empress Jingu|accessdate=2024-10-12}}.}}. In the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'', it is said that after [[:en:Silla|Silla]] surrendered, the remaining two nations of the [[:en:Three Han|Three Han]] (Baekje and Goguryeo) also fell under Japanese control, hence the name "Three Han Expedition." However, as direct battles are recorded only against Silla, it is also referred to as the "Silla Expedition." In the ''[[Kojiki]]'', the submission of Silla and Baekje is mentioned, but there is no record of Goguryeo's reaction, and the term "Three Han" does not appear. In the ''[[Kokushi Daijiten (Shōwa era)|Kokushi Daijiten]]'' published by Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, it is listed under the entry "Silla Expedition Narrative." The "Three Han" refers to [[:en:Mahan|Mahan]] (later Baekje), [[:en:Byeonhan|Byeonhan]] (later [[:en:Imna|Imna]] and [[:en:Gaya|Gaya]]), and [[:en:Jinhan|Jinhan]] (later Silla), excluding Goguryeo and representing only the southern part of the Korean Peninsula. == Overview == {{Stub|date=2012nd year 1月}} {{See|Empress Jingu|Nihon Shoki}} The following is an overview of the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' account. === Oracle at Kashii Shrine and Chūai Tennō === In the 8th year of Chūai Tennō's reign (199 AD), Chūai Tennō visited Kashii Palace (modern-day [[Kashii Shrine]]) in Fukuoka's Hakata region with [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]] to subjugate the [[Kumaso]] tribe. At Kashii Palace, Empress Jingu became possessed by a deity and received a divine revelation. The oracle instructed them to attack [[:en:Silla|Silla]], a land rich with treasures, instead of the Kumaso. However, Chūai Tennō did not believe the oracle, climbed a high hill, and looked out at the sea, asking why the gods would deceive him. The deity then proclaimed that Chūai would not obtain the land but that his offspring would accomplish it. Disregarding the oracle, Chūai Tennō attacked the Kumaso but was defeated and retreated. In the 9th year of his reign (200 AD), he passed away at Kashii Palace in Tsukushi. The empress and others lamented that his death was due to ignoring the divine revelation. His body was transported by sea to Toyoura Palace for temporary burial by [[Takenouchi no Sukune]]. In the ''Amatsufumi,'' it is recorded that Chūai Tennō was struck by a Kumaso arrow. === Empress Jingu’s Expedition to Silla === [[Image:EmpressJinguInKorea.jpg|thumb|350 px|Korean Expedition. Painted by [[:en:Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|Tsukioka Yoshitoshi]] in 1880.]] [[Image:UtagawaKuniyoshiKaibyaku.jpg|thumb|350 px|Silla King submitting to Empress Jingu. Painted by [[Utagawa Kuniyoshi]] in 1860.]] After the sudden death of her husband Chūai Tennō (200 AD), Empress Jingu administered the government from 201 to 269 AD. In March of the 9th year of Chūai Tennō's reign, she entered the [[Saikū]] (sacred palace) as a high priestess and first subdued the Kumaso. In September, she gathered her forces and set out for the Korean Peninsula, acting on a second divine oracle from [[Sumiyoshi no Ōkami]]. Pregnant with her child (the future Ōjin Tennō), she crossed the sea to attack [[:en:Silla|Silla]]. The kingdom surrendered without resistance, promising tribute and allegiance. Goguryeo and Baekje also pledged allegiance. During the voyage, Empress Jingu delayed childbirth by cooling her abdomen with stones called [[Tsukiyome Stones]] and [[Chinkai Stones]]. These stones were later enshrined at shrines such as [[Tsukiyomi Shrine (Iki)|Tsukiyomi Shrine]] in Iki City, Nagasaki Prefecture, and [[Chinkai Stone Hachiman Shrine]] in Itoshima City, Fukuoka Prefecture. After returning to Japan, Empress Jingu gave birth to Ōjin Tennō in Umi, Tsukushi, and changed his swaddling clothes in Shime. As a token of her conquest of Silla, she deposited a banner with eight streams at the summit of Tsushima (present-day [[Kaijin Shrine]]). The empress returned to the Kinai region after the expedition. However, her son’s half-brothers, [[Kozaka no Miko]] and [[Oshikuma no Miko]], rebelled against her in Kinai. The rebellion was suppressed by forces led by [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] and [[Tatekurakuma no Mikoto]]. The above is the core narrative shared between the ''[[Kojiki]]'' and the ''[[Nihon Shoki]].'' According to the ''Nihon Shoki,'' in addition to Silla, Goguryeo and Baekje also pledged allegiance. Silla’s king offered his prince, Misikochihatori Kan-gi, as a hostage. == Notes == * Empress Jingu is considered an important but legendary figure in Japanese history. Many aspects of her story have been examined for historical accuracy and symbolic interpretation {{translated page|ja|三韓征伐|version=104412695|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Completion tier 1]] }} [[sn:Three Han Campaign]] [[ja:三韓征伐]] [[ja:https://shinto.miraheze.org/wiki/Three Han Campaign?wpcategory=ZZZZZZZZZ+Unlinked#:~:text=Han%20Expedition%20(-,%E4%B8%89%E9%9F%93%E5%BE%81%E4%BC%90%2C,-Sankan%20Seibatsu)%20refers]] [[Category:Pseudohistory]] [[Category:Japan–Korea Relations in Antiquity]] [[Category:Kofun period]] [[Category:Historiography of Japan]] [[Category:Wars involving Japan]] [[Category:Wars involving Korea]] [[Category:Empress Jingū]] [[ko:삼한 정벌]] [[zh:三韩征伐]]

It was further embellished by the ideology of the ancient imperial system in the 7th to 8th centuries and finally established in the Chronicles of Japan." {{cite kotobank|encyclopedia=Shogakukan Encyclopedia of Japan (Nipponica)|author=Yosinobu Tsukaguchi|word=Empress Jingu|accessdate=2024-10-12}}.}}{{refnest|group="注"|According to Yamakawa Publishing's "Yamakawa Dictionary of Japanese History, Revised Edition," Empress Jingu is a character in the Chronicles of Japan, and the narrative of the Korean expedition "was likely compiled in its present form after the late 6th century. However, it is also noted that some articles in the Chronicles of Japan regarding relations with the Korean Peninsula, such as the story of the "Seven-Branched Sword" being presented from Baekje, align with historical facts when adjusted by 120 years (two cycles of the Chinese sexagenary cycle)." {{cite kotobank|encyclopedia=Yamakawa Dictionary of Japanese History, Revised Edition|word=Empress Jingu|accessdate=2024-10-12}}.}}. In the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'', it is said that after [[:en:Silla|Silla]] surrendered, the remaining two nations of the [[:en:Three Han|Three Han]] (Baekje and Goguryeo) also fell under Japanese control, hence the name "Three Han Expedition." However, as direct battles are recorded only against Silla, it is also referred to as the "Silla Expedition." In the ''[[Kojiki]]'', the submission of Silla and Baekje is mentioned, but there is no record of Goguryeo's reaction, and the term "Three Han" does not appear. In the ''[[Kokushi Daijiten (Shōwa era)|Kokushi Daijiten]]'' published by Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, it is listed under the entry "Silla Expedition Narrative." The "Three Han" refers to [[:en:Mahan|Mahan]] (later Baekje), [[:en:Byeonhan|Byeonhan]] (later [[:en:Imna|Imna]] and [[:en:Gaya|Gaya]]), and [[:en:Jinhan|Jinhan]] (later Silla), excluding Goguryeo and representing only the southern part of the Korean Peninsula. == Overview == {{Stub|date=2012nd year 1月}} {{See|Empress Jingu|Nihon Shoki}} The following is an overview of the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' account. === Oracle at Kashii Shrine and Chūai Tennō === In the 8th year of Chūai Tennō's reign (199 AD), Chūai Tennō visited Kashii Palace (modern-day [[Kashii Shrine]]) in Fukuoka's Hakata region with [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]] to subjugate the [[Kumaso]] tribe. At Kashii Palace, Empress Jingu became possessed by a deity and received a divine revelation. The oracle instructed them to attack [[:en:Silla|Silla]], a land rich with treasures, instead of the Kumaso. However, Chūai Tennō did not believe the oracle, climbed a high hill, and looked out at the sea, asking why the gods would deceive him. The deity then proclaimed that Chūai would not obtain the land but that his offspring would accomplish it. Disregarding the oracle, Chūai Tennō attacked the Kumaso but was defeated and retreated. In the 9th year of his reign (200 AD), he passed away at Kashii Palace in Tsukushi. The empress and others lamented that his death was due to ignoring the divine revelation. His body was transported by sea to Toyoura Palace for temporary burial by [[Takenouchi no Sukune]]. In the ''Amatsufumi,'' it is recorded that Chūai Tennō was struck by a Kumaso arrow. === Empress Jingu’s Expedition to Silla === [[Image:EmpressJinguInKorea.jpg|thumb|350 px|Korean Expedition. Painted by [[:en:Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|Tsukioka Yoshitoshi]] in 1880.]] [[Image:UtagawaKuniyoshiKaibyaku.jpg|thumb|350 px|Silla King submitting to Empress Jingu. Painted by [[Utagawa Kuniyoshi]] in 1860.]] After the sudden death of her husband Chūai Tennō (200 AD), Empress Jingu administered the government from 201 to 269 AD. In March of the 9th year of Chūai Tennō's reign, she entered the [[Saikū]] (sacred palace) as a high priestess and first subdued the Kumaso. In September, she gathered her forces and set out for the Korean Peninsula, acting on a second divine oracle from [[Sumiyoshi no Ōkami]]. Pregnant with her child (the future Ōjin Tennō), she crossed the sea to attack [[:en:Silla|Silla]]. The kingdom surrendered without resistance, promising tribute and allegiance. Goguryeo and Baekje also pledged allegiance. During the voyage, Empress Jingu delayed childbirth by cooling her abdomen with stones called [[Tsukiyome Stones]] and [[Chinkai Stones]]. These stones were later enshrined at shrines such as [[Tsukiyomi Shrine (Iki)|Tsukiyomi Shrine]] in Iki City, Nagasaki Prefecture, and [[Chinkai Stone Hachiman Shrine]] in Itoshima City, Fukuoka Prefecture. After returning to Japan, Empress Jingu gave birth to Ōjin Tennō in Umi, Tsukushi, and changed his swaddling clothes in Shime. As a token of her conquest of Silla, she deposited a banner with eight streams at the summit of Tsushima (present-day [[Kaijin Shrine]]). The empress returned to the Kinai region after the expedition. However, her son’s half-brothers, [[Kozaka no Miko]] and [[Oshikuma no Miko]], rebelled against her in Kinai. The rebellion was suppressed by forces led by [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] and [[Tatekurakuma no Mikoto]]. The above is the core narrative shared between the ''[[Kojiki]]'' and the ''[[Nihon Shoki]].'' According to the ''Nihon Shoki,'' in addition to Silla, Goguryeo and Baekje also pledged allegiance. Silla’s king offered his prince, Misikochihatori Kan-gi, as a hostage. == Notes == * Empress Jingu is considered an important but legendary figure in Japanese history. Many aspects of her story have been examined for historical accuracy and symbolic interpretation {{translated page|ja|三韓征伐|version=104412695|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Completion tier 1]] }} [[ja:三韓征伐]] [[ja:https://shinto.miraheze.org/wiki/Three Han Campaign?wpcategory=ZZZZZZZZZ+Unlinked#:~:text=Han%20Expedition%20(-,%E4%B8%89%E9%9F%93%E5%BE%81%E4%BC%90%2C,-Sankan%20Seibatsu)%20refers]] [[Category:Pseudohistory]] [[Category:Japan–Korea Relations in Antiquity]] [[Category:Kofun period]] [[Category:Historiography of Japan]] [[Category:Wars involving Japan]] [[Category:Wars involving Korea]] [[Category:Empress Jingū]] [[ko:삼한 정벌]] [[zh:三韩征伐]] {{wikidata link|Q11249435}}

It was further embellished by the ideology of the ancient imperial system in the 7th to 8th centuries and finally established in the Chronicles of Japan." {{cite kotobank|encyclopedia=Shogakukan Encyclopedia of Japan (Nipponica)|author=Yosinobu Tsukaguchi|word=Empress Jingu|accessdate=2024-10-12}}.}}{{refnest|group="注"|According to Yamakawa Publishing's "Yamakawa Dictionary of Japanese History, Revised Edition," Empress Jingu is a character in the Chronicles of Japan, and the narrative of the Korean expedition "was likely compiled in its present form after the late 6th century. However, it is also noted that some articles in the Chronicles of Japan regarding relations with the Korean Peninsula, such as the story of the "Seven-Branched Sword" being presented from Baekje, align with historical facts when adjusted by 120 years (two cycles of the Chinese sexagenary cycle)." {{cite kotobank|encyclopedia=Yamakawa Dictionary of Japanese History, Revised Edition|word=Empress Jingu|accessdate=2024-10-12}}.}}. In the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'', it is said that after [[:en:Silla|Silla]] surrendered, the remaining two nations of the [[:en:Three Han|Three Han]] (Baekje and Goguryeo) also fell under Japanese control, hence the name "Three Han Expedition." However, as direct battles are recorded only against Silla, it is also referred to as the "Silla Expedition." In the ''[[Kojiki]]'', the submission of Silla and Baekje is mentioned, but there is no record of Goguryeo's reaction, and the term "Three Han" does not appear. In the ''[[Kokushi Daijiten (Shōwa era)|Kokushi Daijiten]]'' published by Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, it is listed under the entry "Silla Expedition Narrative." The "Three Han" refers to [[:en:Mahan|Mahan]] (later Baekje), [[:en:Byeonhan|Byeonhan]] (later [[:en:Imna|Imna]] and [[:en:Gaya|Gaya]]), and [[:en:Jinhan|Jinhan]] (later Silla), excluding Goguryeo and representing only the southern part of the Korean Peninsula. == Overview == {{Stub|date=2012nd year 1月}} {{See|Empress Jingu|Nihon Shoki}} The following is an overview of the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' account. === Oracle at Kashii Shrine and Chūai Tennō === In the 8th year of Chūai Tennō's reign (199 AD), Chūai Tennō visited Kashii Palace (modern-day [[Kashii Shrine]]) in Fukuoka's Hakata region with [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]] to subjugate the [[Kumaso]] tribe. At Kashii Palace, Empress Jingu became possessed by a deity and received a divine revelation. The oracle instructed them to attack [[:en:Silla|Silla]], a land rich with treasures, instead of the Kumaso. However, Chūai Tennō did not believe the oracle, climbed a high hill, and looked out at the sea, asking why the gods would deceive him. The deity then proclaimed that Chūai would not obtain the land but that his offspring would accomplish it. Disregarding the oracle, Chūai Tennō attacked the Kumaso but was defeated and retreated. In the 9th year of his reign (200 AD), he passed away at Kashii Palace in Tsukushi. The empress and others lamented that his death was due to ignoring the divine revelation. His body was transported by sea to Toyoura Palace for temporary burial by [[Takenouchi no Sukune]]. In the ''Amatsufumi,'' it is recorded that Chūai Tennō was struck by a Kumaso arrow. === Empress Jingu’s Expedition to Silla === [[Image:EmpressJinguInKorea.jpg|thumb|350 px|Korean Expedition. Painted by [[:en:Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|Tsukioka Yoshitoshi]] in 1880.]] [[Image:UtagawaKuniyoshiKaibyaku.jpg|thumb|350 px|Silla King submitting to Empress Jingu. Painted by [[Utagawa Kuniyoshi]] in 1860.]] After the sudden death of her husband Chūai Tennō (200 AD), Empress Jingu administered the government from 201 to 269 AD. In March of the 9th year of Chūai Tennō's reign, she entered the [[Saikū]] (sacred palace) as a high priestess and first subdued the Kumaso. In September, she gathered her forces and set out for the Korean Peninsula, acting on a second divine oracle from [[Sumiyoshi no Ōkami]]. Pregnant with her child (the future Ōjin Tennō), she crossed the sea to attack [[:en:Silla|Silla]]. The kingdom surrendered without resistance, promising tribute and allegiance. Goguryeo and Baekje also pledged allegiance. During the voyage, Empress Jingu delayed childbirth by cooling her abdomen with stones called [[Tsukiyome Stones]] and [[Chinkai Stones]]. These stones were later enshrined at shrines such as [[Tsukiyomi Shrine (Iki)|Tsukiyomi Shrine]] in Iki City, Nagasaki Prefecture, and [[Chinkai Stone Hachiman Shrine]] in Itoshima City, Fukuoka Prefecture. After returning to Japan, Empress Jingu gave birth to Ōjin Tennō in Umi, Tsukushi, and changed his swaddling clothes in Shime. As a token of her conquest of Silla, she deposited a banner with eight streams at the summit of Tsushima (present-day [[Kaijin Shrine]]). The empress returned to the Kinai region after the expedition. However, her son’s half-brothers, [[Kozaka no Miko]] and [[Oshikuma no Miko]], rebelled against her in Kinai. The rebellion was suppressed by forces led by [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] and [[Tatekurakuma no Mikoto]]. The above is the core narrative shared between the ''[[Kojiki]]'' and the ''[[Nihon Shoki]].'' According to the ''Nihon Shoki,'' in addition to Silla, Goguryeo and Baekje also pledged allegiance. Silla’s king offered his prince, Misikochihatori Kan-gi, as a hostage. == Notes == * Empress Jingu is considered an important but legendary figure in Japanese history. Many aspects of her story have been examined for historical accuracy and symbolic interpretation {{translated page|ja|三韓征伐|version=104412695|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Completion tier 1]] }} [[ja:三韓征伐]] [[ja:https://shinto.miraheze.org/wiki/Three Han Campaign?wpcategory=ZZZZZZZZZ+Unlinked#:~:text=Han%20Expedition%20(-,%E4%B8%89%E9%9F%93%E5%BE%81%E4%BC%90%2C,-Sankan%20Seibatsu)%20refers]] [[Category:Pseudohistory]] [[Category:Japan–Korea Relations in Antiquity]] [[Category:Kofun period]] [[Category:Historiography of Japan]] [[Category:Wars involving Japan]] [[Category:Wars involving Korea]] [[Category:Empress Jingū]] [[ko:삼한 정벌]] [[zh:三韩征伐]] {{wikidata link|Q11249435}} [[Category:Wikidata no short description]]

[[:en:Silla|Silla]] | commander1 = [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]] | commander2 = Unknown | strength1 = Unknown | strength2 = Unknown | casualties1 = Unknown | casualties2 = Unknown }} '''Three Han Expedition''' (三韓征伐, ''Sankan Seibatsu'') refers to a Japanese legend in which [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]], the consort of [[:en:Chūai Tennō|Chūai Tennō]] and the mother of [[:en:Ōjin Tennō|Ōjin Tennō]], invaded [[:en:Silla|Silla]] following the death of Chūai Tennō and subjugated a wide area of the [[:en:Korea|Korea]] (the [[:en:Three Han|Three Han]]) {{refnest|group="注"|According to Yoriko Kurazuka, [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]] is described as "the consort of [[:en:Chūai Tennō|Chūai Tennō]], the protagonist of the '''Silla expedition legend''' in the Chronicles of Japan, and the mother of [[:en:Ōjin Tennō|Ōjin Tennō]]." {{cite kotobank|encyclopedia=Sekai Daihyakka Jiten |word=Empress Jingu|accessdate=2024-10-12}}.}}{{refnest|group="注"|According to Yosinobu Tsukaguchi, a Ph.D. in literature and historian, the Empress Jingu legend is "a narrative of invasion of the Korean Peninsula transmitted by the court, incorporating folk traditions based on mother-and-child deity worship and the traditions of the ancient Ohotarashihime clan residing in Tsuzuki District, Kyoto Prefecture. It was further embellished by the ideology of the ancient imperial system in the 7th to 8th centuries and finally established in the Chronicles of Japan." {{cite kotobank|encyclopedia=Shogakukan Encyclopedia of Japan (Nipponica)|author=Yosinobu Tsukaguchi|word=Empress Jingu|accessdate=2024-10-12}}.}}{{refnest|group="注"|According to Yamakawa Publishing's "Yamakawa Dictionary of Japanese History, Revised Edition," Empress Jingu is a character in the Chronicles of Japan, and the narrative of the Korean expedition "was likely compiled in its present form after the late 6th century. However, it is also noted that some articles in the Chronicles of Japan regarding relations with the Korean Peninsula, such as the story of the "Seven-Branched Sword" being presented from Baekje, align with historical facts when adjusted by 120 years (two cycles of the Chinese sexagenary cycle)." {{cite kotobank|encyclopedia=Yamakawa Dictionary of Japanese History, Revised Edition|word=Empress Jingu|accessdate=2024-10-12}}.}}. In the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'', it is said that after [[:en:Silla|Silla]] surrendered, the remaining two nations of the [[:en:Three Han|Three Han]] (Baekje and Goguryeo) also fell under Japanese control, hence the name "Three Han Expedition." However, as direct battles are recorded only against Silla, it is also referred to as the "Silla Expedition." In the ''[[Kojiki]]'', the submission of Silla and Baekje is mentioned, but there is no record of Goguryeo's reaction, and the term "Three Han" does not appear. In the ''[[Kokushi Daijiten (Shōwa era)|Kokushi Daijiten]]'' published by Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, it is listed under the entry "Silla Expedition Narrative." The "Three Han" refers to [[:en:Mahan|Mahan]] (later Baekje), [[:en:Byeonhan|Byeonhan]] (later [[:en:Imna|Imna]] and [[:en:Gaya|Gaya]]), and [[:en:Jinhan|Jinhan]] (later Silla), excluding Goguryeo and representing only the southern part of the Korean Peninsula. == Overview == {{Stub|date=2012nd year 1月}} {{See|Empress Jingu|Nihon Shoki}} The following is an overview of the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' account. === Oracle at Kashii Shrine and Chūai Tennō === In the 8th year of Chūai Tennō's reign (199 AD), Chūai Tennō visited Kashii Palace (modern-day [[Kashii Shrine]]) in Fukuoka's Hakata region with [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]] to subjugate the [[Kumaso]] tribe. At Kashii Palace, Empress Jingu became possessed by a deity and received a divine revelation. The oracle instructed them to attack [[:en:Silla|Silla]], a land rich with treasures, instead of the Kumaso. However, Chūai Tennō did not believe the oracle, climbed a high hill, and looked out at the sea, asking why the gods would deceive him. The deity then proclaimed that Chūai would not obtain the land but that his offspring would accomplish it. Disregarding the oracle, Chūai Tennō attacked the Kumaso but was defeated and retreated. In the 9th year of his reign (200 AD), he passed away at Kashii Palace in Tsukushi. The empress and others lamented that his death was due to ignoring the divine revelation. His body was transported by sea to Toyoura Palace for temporary burial by [[Takenouchi no Sukune]]. In the ''Amatsufumi,'' it is recorded that Chūai Tennō was struck by a Kumaso arrow. === Empress Jingu’s Expedition to Silla === [[Image:EmpressJinguInKorea.jpg|thumb|350 px|Korean Expedition. Painted by [[:en:Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|Tsukioka Yoshitoshi]] in 1880.]] [[Image:UtagawaKuniyoshiKaibyaku.jpg|thumb|350 px|Silla King submitting to Empress Jingu. Painted by [[Utagawa Kuniyoshi]] in 1860.]] After the sudden death of her husband Chūai Tennō (200 AD), Empress Jingu administered the government from 201 to 269 AD. In March of the 9th year of Chūai Tennō's reign, she entered the [[Saikū]] (sacred palace) as a high priestess and first subdued the Kumaso. In September, she gathered her forces and set out for the Korean Peninsula, acting on a second divine oracle from [[Sumiyoshi no Ōkami]]. Pregnant with her child (the future Ōjin Tennō), she crossed the sea to attack [[:en:Silla|Silla]]. The kingdom surrendered without resistance, promising tribute and allegiance. Goguryeo and Baekje also pledged allegiance. During the voyage, Empress Jingu delayed childbirth by cooling her abdomen with stones called [[Tsukiyome Stones]] and [[Chinkai Stones]]. These stones were later enshrined at shrines such as [[Tsukiyomi Shrine (Iki)|Tsukiyomi Shrine]] in Iki City, Nagasaki Prefecture, and [[Chinkai Stone Hachiman Shrine]] in Itoshima City, Fukuoka Prefecture. After returning to Japan, Empress Jingu gave birth to Ōjin Tennō in Umi, Tsukushi, and changed his swaddling clothes in Shime. As a token of her conquest of Silla, she deposited a banner with eight streams at the summit of Tsushima (present-day [[Kaijin Shrine]]). The empress returned to the Kinai region after the expedition. However, her son’s half-brothers, [[Kozaka no Miko]] and [[Oshikuma no Miko]], rebelled against her in Kinai. The rebellion was suppressed by forces led by [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] and [[Tatekurakuma no Mikoto]]. The above is the core narrative shared between the ''[[Kojiki]]'' and the ''[[Nihon Shoki]].'' According to the ''Nihon Shoki,'' in addition to Silla, Goguryeo and Baekje also pledged allegiance. Silla’s king offered his prince, Misikochihatori Kan-gi, as a hostage. == Notes == * Empress Jingu is considered an important but legendary figure in Japanese history. Many aspects of her story have been examined for historical accuracy and symbolic interpretation {{translated page|ja|三韓征伐|version=104412695|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Completion tier 1]] }} [[ja:三韓征伐]] [[ja:https://shinto.miraheze.org/wiki/Three Han Campaign?wpcategory=ZZZZZZZZZ+Unlinked#:~:text=Han%20Expedition%20(-,%E4%B8%89%E9%9F%93%E5%BE%81%E4%BC%90%2C,-Sankan%20Seibatsu)%20refers]] [[Category:Pseudohistory]] [[Category:Japan–Korea Relations in Antiquity]] [[Category:Kofun period]] [[Category:Historiography of Japan]] [[Category:Wars involving Japan]] [[Category:Wars involving Korea]] [[Category:Empress Jingū]] [[ko:삼한 정벌]] [[zh:三韩征伐]] {{wikidata link|Q11249435}} [[Category:Wikidata no short description]] [[Category:Wikidata has English label]] {{wikidata link|Q11249435}} [[Category:LINKED FROM WIKIDATA DO NOT OVERWRITE]][[Category:LINKED FROM WIKIDATA DO NOT OVERWRITE]]

[[:en:Silla|Silla]] | commander1 = [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]] | commander2 = Unknown | strength1 = Unknown | strength2 = Unknown | casualties1 = Unknown | casualties2 = Unknown }} '''Three Han Expedition''' (三韓征伐, ''Sankan Seibatsu'') refers to a Japanese legend in which [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]], the consort of [[:en:Chūai Tennō|Chūai Tennō]] and the mother of [[:en:Ōjin Tennō|Ōjin Tennō]], invaded [[:en:Silla|Silla]] following the death of Chūai Tennō and subjugated a wide area of the [[:en:Korea|Korea]] (the [[:en:Three Han|Three Han]]) {{refnest|group="注"|According to Yoriko Kurazuka, [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]] is described as "the consort of [[:en:Chūai Tennō|Chūai Tennō]], the protagonist of the '''Silla expedition legend''' in the Chronicles of Japan, and the mother of [[:en:Ōjin Tennō|Ōjin Tennō]]." {{cite kotobank|encyclopedia=Sekai Daihyakka Jiten |word=Empress Jingu|accessdate=2024-10-12}}.}}{{refnest|group="注"|According to Yosinobu Tsukaguchi, a Ph.D. in literature and historian, the Empress Jingu legend is "a narrative of invasion of the Korean Peninsula transmitted by the court, incorporating folk traditions based on mother-and-child deity worship and the traditions of the ancient Ohotarashihime clan residing in Tsuzuki District, Kyoto Prefecture. It was further embellished by the ideology of the ancient imperial system in the 7th to 8th centuries and finally established in the Chronicles of Japan." {{cite kotobank|encyclopedia=Shogakukan Encyclopedia of Japan (Nipponica)|author=Yosinobu Tsukaguchi|word=Empress Jingu|accessdate=2024-10-12}}.}}{{refnest|group="注"|According to Yamakawa Publishing's "Yamakawa Dictionary of Japanese History, Revised Edition," Empress Jingu is a character in the Chronicles of Japan, and the narrative of the Korean expedition "was likely compiled in its present form after the late 6th century. However, it is also noted that some articles in the Chronicles of Japan regarding relations with the Korean Peninsula, such as the story of the "Seven-Branched Sword" being presented from Baekje, align with historical facts when adjusted by 120 years (two cycles of the Chinese sexagenary cycle)." {{cite kotobank|encyclopedia=Yamakawa Dictionary of Japanese History, Revised Edition|word=Empress Jingu|accessdate=2024-10-12}}.}}. In the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'', it is said that after [[:en:Silla|Silla]] surrendered, the remaining two nations of the [[:en:Three Han|Three Han]] (Baekje and Goguryeo) also fell under Japanese control, hence the name "Three Han Expedition." However, as direct battles are recorded only against Silla, it is also referred to as the "Silla Expedition." In the ''[[Kojiki]]'', the submission of Silla and Baekje is mentioned, but there is no record of Goguryeo's reaction, and the term "Three Han" does not appear. In the ''[[Kokushi Daijiten (Shōwa era)|Kokushi Daijiten]]'' published by Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, it is listed under the entry "Silla Expedition Narrative." The "Three Han" refers to [[:en:Mahan|Mahan]] (later Baekje), [[:en:Byeonhan|Byeonhan]] (later [[:en:Imna|Imna]] and [[:en:Gaya|Gaya]]), and [[:en:Jinhan|Jinhan]] (later Silla), excluding Goguryeo and representing only the southern part of the Korean Peninsula. == Overview == {{Stub|date=2012nd year 1月}} {{See|Empress Jingu|Nihon Shoki}} The following is an overview of the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' account. === Oracle at Kashii Shrine and Chūai Tennō === In the 8th year of Chūai Tennō's reign (199 AD), Chūai Tennō visited Kashii Palace (modern-day [[Kashii Shrine]]) in Fukuoka's Hakata region with [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]] to subjugate the [[Kumaso]] tribe. At Kashii Palace, Empress Jingu became possessed by a deity and received a divine revelation. The oracle instructed them to attack [[:en:Silla|Silla]], a land rich with treasures, instead of the Kumaso. However, Chūai Tennō did not believe the oracle, climbed a high hill, and looked out at the sea, asking why the gods would deceive him. The deity then proclaimed that Chūai would not obtain the land but that his offspring would accomplish it. Disregarding the oracle, Chūai Tennō attacked the Kumaso but was defeated and retreated. In the 9th year of his reign (200 AD), he passed away at Kashii Palace in Tsukushi. The empress and others lamented that his death was due to ignoring the divine revelation. His body was transported by sea to Toyoura Palace for temporary burial by [[Takenouchi no Sukune]]. In the ''Amatsufumi,'' it is recorded that Chūai Tennō was struck by a Kumaso arrow. === Empress Jingu’s Expedition to Silla === [[Image:EmpressJinguInKorea.jpg|thumb|350 px|Korean Expedition. Painted by [[:en:Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|Tsukioka Yoshitoshi]] in 1880.]] [[Image:UtagawaKuniyoshiKaibyaku.jpg|thumb|350 px|Silla King submitting to Empress Jingu. Painted by [[Utagawa Kuniyoshi]] in 1860.]] After the sudden death of her husband Chūai Tennō (200 AD), Empress Jingu administered the government from 201 to 269 AD. In March of the 9th year of Chūai Tennō's reign, she entered the [[Saikū]] (sacred palace) as a high priestess and first subdued the Kumaso. In September, she gathered her forces and set out for the Korean Peninsula, acting on a second divine oracle from [[Sumiyoshi no Ōkami]]. Pregnant with her child (the future Ōjin Tennō), she crossed the sea to attack [[:en:Silla|Silla]]. The kingdom surrendered without resistance, promising tribute and allegiance. Goguryeo and Baekje also pledged allegiance. During the voyage, Empress Jingu delayed childbirth by cooling her abdomen with stones called [[Tsukiyome Stones]] and [[Chinkai Stones]]. These stones were later enshrined at shrines such as [[Tsukiyomi Shrine (Iki)|Tsukiyomi Shrine]] in Iki City, Nagasaki Prefecture, and [[Chinkai Stone Hachiman Shrine]] in Itoshima City, Fukuoka Prefecture. After returning to Japan, Empress Jingu gave birth to Ōjin Tennō in Umi, Tsukushi, and changed his swaddling clothes in Shime. As a token of her conquest of Silla, she deposited a banner with eight streams at the summit of Tsushima (present-day [[Kaijin Shrine]]). The empress returned to the Kinai region after the expedition. However, her son’s half-brothers, [[Kozaka no Miko]] and [[Oshikuma no Miko]], rebelled against her in Kinai. The rebellion was suppressed by forces led by [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] and [[Tatekurakuma no Mikoto]]. The above is the core narrative shared between the ''[[Kojiki]]'' and the ''[[Nihon Shoki]].'' According to the ''Nihon Shoki,'' in addition to Silla, Goguryeo and Baekje also pledged allegiance. Silla’s king offered his prince, Misikochihatori Kan-gi, as a hostage. == Notes == * Empress Jingu is considered an important but legendary figure in Japanese history. Many aspects of her story have been examined for historical accuracy and symbolic interpretation {{translated page|ja|三韓征伐|version=104412695|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Completion tier 1]] }} [[ja:三韓征伐]] [[ja:https://shinto.miraheze.org/wiki/Three Han Campaign?wpcategory=ZZZZZZZZZ+Unlinked#:~:text=Han%20Expedition%20(-,%E4%B8%89%E9%9F%93%E5%BE%81%E4%BC%90%2C,-Sankan%20Seibatsu)%20refers]] [[Category:Pseudohistory]] [[Category:Japan–Korea Relations in Antiquity]] [[Category:Kofun period]] [[Category:Historiography of Japan]] [[Category:Wars involving Japan]] [[Category:Wars involving Korea]] [[Category:Empress Jingū]] [[ko:삼한 정벌]] [[zh:三韩征伐]] {{wikidata link|Q11249435}} [[Category:Wikidata no short description]] [[Category:Wikidata has English label]] {{wikidata link|Q11249435}} [[Category:LINKED FROM WIKIDATA DO NOT OVERWRITE]][[Category:LINKED FROM WIKIDATA DO NOT OVERWRITE]][[Category:LINKED FROM WIKIDATA DO NOT OVERWRITE]][[Category:LINKED FROM WIKIDATA DO NOT OVERWRITE]][[Category:LINKED FROM WIKIDATA DO NOT OVERWRITE]]
